q: What does the abbreviation DBMS stand for?
x: A DBMS is software that is used to create, store and manage databases. Examples include MySQL and Oracle.

q: Which constraint ensures that a column cannot contain empty (NULL) values?
x: NOT NULL forces every record to have a value. UNIQUE prevents duplicates but, depending on the system, may still allow NULL.

q: Which of the following describes a one-to-many relationship?
o: One teacher teaches many students in a class
One student has exactly one roll number
Many students use many books in a library
One country has exactly one capital city
x: One record on the "one" side relates to several records on the "many" side. The second option is one-to-one and the third is many-to-many.

q: What is meant by redundancy in a database?
o: Unnecessary repetition of the same data
Loss of the database due to power failure
Use of too many primary keys
x: Redundancy wastes space and can cause inconsistent copies. Normalisation reduces it.

q: In a relational database, data is stored in:
x: The relational model organises data into tables made of rows and columns. Stacks and queues are different data structures used in programs.

q: A table is in First Normal Form (1NF) when:
o: Every field contains only atomic (single) values
It has no foreign keys at all
It contains only one record in total
Every field in it holds a number only
x: 1NF requires indivisible values with no repeating groups. A cell such as "Maths, Physics" violates it.

q: How is a many-to-many relationship, such as Students and Courses, normally implemented in a relational database?
o: By placing a repeated list of courses in the Student table
By merging both tables into one column
With a third (junction) table holding both keys
By using two primary keys in each table
x: A junction table has a foreign key to each side, turning the many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships. Storing a list in one column breaks 1NF.

q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of the traditional file-processing approach compared with a database?
o: Better sharing of data between users
Centralised security of all the data
x: In separate files, the same data is repeated in many places and copies can disagree. A DBMS reduces this and offers sharing and security.

q: A row in a table is also known as a:
x: A row (tuple) holds all the data about one entity. A column or field holds one attribute of all entities.

q: A table is in Second Normal Form (2NF) when it is in 1NF and:
o: It has no foreign key in any column
It has no transitive dependency among columns
It contains only a single column in total
It has no partial dependency on a composite key
x: 2NF removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite primary key. Removing transitive dependencies is the extra requirement of 3NF.

q: In an ER diagram, an entity is normally drawn as a:
x: Entities are rectangles, attributes are ovals and relationships are diamonds.

q: A column in a table is also known as a:
x: A column, also called an attribute, holds one kind of data, such as Name. Record and tuple mean a row, and a relation means the whole table.

q: A table is in Third Normal Form (3NF) when it is in 2NF and:
o: Every attribute depends on only part of the key
The table has been given no primary key
No non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
All of the attributes of the table are keys
x: 3NF removes transitive dependencies, such as City determining Province when both are stored in a student table.

q: In an ER diagram, a relationship between entities is drawn as a:
x: A diamond joins the related entities and is labelled with the verb, such as "enrols". Rectangles represent the entities.

q: Which key is chosen to uniquely identify each record in a table?
x: A primary key has unique, non-null values for every record. A foreign key only refers to a primary key in another table, so it may repeat.

q: Which of the following is an anomaly caused by poor table design?
x: Insertion, update and deletion anomalies arise when the same fact is stored in many places. Changing it in one record only would leave data inconsistent.

q: What does ER stand for in an ER diagram?
x: An ER diagram shows entities, their attributes and the relationships between them.

q: Which of the following is a Data Definition Language (DDL) command?
x: DDL commands such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP define the structure of the database. INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE are Data Manipulation commands.

q: A table has the columns (OrderID, ProductID, ProductName, Quantity) with the key (OrderID, ProductID). ProductName depends only on ProductID. Which normal form is violated?
x: ProductName depends on only part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency, and that is what 2NF forbids. The values are atomic, so 1NF is satisfied.

q: Which of the following is a Data Manipulation Language (DML) command?
x: UPDATE changes the data stored in rows, so it is DML. ALTER, CREATE and DROP change the structure and are DDL.

q: A foreign key is used to:
o: Encrypt all the data in the table
Sort the records into alphabetical order
Delete the duplicate copies of tables
Link a column to the primary key of another table
x: A foreign key holds values that must exist as the primary key in the related table, which enforces the relationship between the tables.

q: What is a candidate key?
o: A column whose value is always NULL
The key chosen only for sorting the rows
A column or set of columns that could serve as the primary key
A key that points to another database
x: Candidate keys are minimal attributes that uniquely identify a record. One of them is chosen as the primary key and the rest are alternate keys.

q: The number of columns (attributes) in a table is called its:
x: Degree counts the attributes and cardinality counts the tuples (rows). A table with 5 columns and 30 rows has degree 5 and cardinality 30.

q: A table has 4 columns and 25 rows. What is its cardinality?
x: Cardinality is the number of rows (tuples). The degree is 4, and 100 is the number of cells.

q: What does the term "data independence" mean?
o: Changing the storage structure does not force changes to application programs
Data can exist without any computer
Each user owns a separate copy of the data
Data never needs to be backed up
x: A database separates logical use from physical storage, so programs keep working even if the storage layout changes.

q: Which person is responsible for the security, backup and performance of a database?
x: The database administrator (DBA) controls access, backups and tuning. End users only use the data.

q: Which of the following is a database model?
x: The relational model is the one used by most systems today. Hierarchical and network models are older database models.

q: The set of all permitted values for an attribute is called its:
x: A domain defines the valid values for a column; for example, the Marks domain may be whole numbers from 0 to 100.

q: Which of the following best describes a database schema?
o: The structure or design of the database
The data stored in the tables at one moment
The password used by the administrator
The list of users who are online
x: The schema describes tables, columns and relationships. The data in the tables at a given moment is called an instance.

q: Which statement about a primary key is NOT true?
o: A table can have only one
x: A primary key must have unique values; duplicates are exactly what it prevents.

q: Which of the following is a DBMS software product?
x: MySQL is a database management system. The others are a media player, a PDF reader and a file compressor.

q: Which key in a student table would be the best primary key?
x: A roll number is unique to each student. Names, cities and birth dates can be shared by several students.

q: Which statement about NULL in a database is correct?
o: NULL means a missing or unknown value
NULL is the same as the number zero
NULL is the same as a space character
NULL is the same as an empty table
x: NULL marks the absence of a value. Zero and a blank string are actual values.

q: Which of the following is true about a composite key?
o: It is a key that is used only in views
It is made of two or more columns taken together
It is a key that may hold NULL values
It is a primary key kept in another database
x: A composite key identifies records by a combination of attributes, such as (StudentID, CourseID) in an enrolment table.

q: A sequential file holds 1000 student records stored one after another. To read the record at position 500, the computer must start from the beginning. How many records does it read before it reaches that record?
x: In a sequential file, every earlier record is read first: records 1 to 499, so 499 come before it. 250 is half of that, as if the search could start in the middle, and 0 would be true only for direct access, which goes straight to the record.

q: Which file organisation calculates the storage address of a record from its key field, so the record is reached without reading any other record?
x: Direct organisation applies a formula (hashing) to the key to get the address. Indexed organisation instead looks the key up in a separate index table.

q: A file keeps a separate table of key values and the addresses of their records. This table is searched first to find a record, like the index at the back of a book. Which organisation is this?
x: Indexed organisation uses an index of keys and addresses to find records. Direct organisation computes the address from the key instead of looking it up.

q: A payroll program processes every employee's record one after another once a month and never needs to find one record quickly. Which organisation is the simplest that suits this job?
x: When all records are processed in order in a batch, sequential organisation is simplest and works well. Direct access is useful only when single records must be reached quickly.

q: A bank's file must be processed in account-number order at the end of each day and must also let a clerk find any single account quickly. Which organisation supports both needs?
x: Indexed sequential keeps records in key order for sequential processing and adds an index for fast single look-ups. A purely sequential file is slow for one record, and a direct file is not kept in key order.

q: A file is stored on magnetic tape. In which way can its records be accessed?
o: Randomly in any order at the same speed
Both directly and through an index
x: Tape is read from one end to the other, so records can only be reached in sequence. Direct and indexed access need a disk, which can jump to any position.

q: In a file-based system, one new field is added to the record layout of the Student file. Every program that reads that file now has to be changed. This limitation is called:
x: In file systems, each program contains the file's record layout, so a layout change forces changes to the programs. Redundancy means the same data being stored more than once.

q: The admissions office keeps its data in files of one format and the accounts office in files of another format. Making one report that combines both is very hard. This problem of file systems is called:
x: Data isolation means data is scattered in separate files and formats, so it is hard to bring together. Data independence is a benefit of a DBMS, not a problem.

q: A student's address is stored in both the Library file and the Accounts file. When the student moves, only the Accounts file is updated, so the two files now show different addresses. What is this result called?
x: When copies of the same fact disagree, the data is inconsistent. Storing the address twice is redundancy, and inconsistency is the problem it led to here.

q: Which order goes from the smallest unit of data to the largest?
x: Characters make up a field (such as Name), fields make up a record (one student), and records make up a file (all students). A record is larger than a field, not smaller.

q: A shop keeps a file of today's sales, which is used at the end of the day to update the customers' balances stored in another file. The file of today's sales is a:
x: A transaction file holds recent events used to update the master file. The file of customers' balances is the master file, because it keeps the lasting data.

q: In data processing, calculating each student's total from the subject marks that were typed in belongs to which stage?
x: Typing the marks is input, working out the totals is processing, and printing the result card is output.

q: Why is adding a new record in its correct place slow in a sequential file that is kept sorted by key?
o: The whole file must first be converted into direct organisation
All records after that place must be moved or copied to a new file
A sorted sequential file cannot store new records at all
Every record before that place must be deleted
x: To keep the order, the records after the insertion point have to be shifted, usually by copying the file into a new one with the record inserted. New records can be added; it is just slow.

q: A direct file stores the record with key k at address k mod 7 (the remainder after dividing by 7). Which pair of keys would be sent to the same address?
x: 15 mod 7 = 1 and 22 mod 7 = 1, so both go to address 1 (a collision). The others differ: 15 and 21 give 1 and 0, 10 and 20 give 3 and 6, 8 and 16 give 1 and 2.

q: In Student(RollNo, CNIC, Name, City), both RollNo and CNIC are unique and never empty for every student. RollNo is chosen as the primary key. What is CNIC called?
x: CNIC could also identify every student, so it is a candidate key, and a candidate key not chosen as primary is an alternate key. It is not a foreign key because it does not refer to another table.

q: In which data model are records arranged as a tree, where each child record has exactly one parent record?
x: The hierarchical model is a tree of parent-child records. The network model lets a child have more than one parent, and the relational model uses tables.

q: In a school database, which of these is an entity rather than an attribute?
x: An entity is a thing about which data is stored, such as a teacher. Date of birth, salary and phone number are attributes that describe a teacher.

q: A database has the tables Class(ClassID, Room) and Student(RollNo, Name, ClassID), where ClassID is the primary key of Class. Which column of Student is a foreign key?
x: ClassID in Student holds values that must match the primary key of Class, so it is a foreign key. RollNo is Student's own primary key, and Room is not in Student.

q: During database design, which step describes the data without depending on any particular DBMS and is usually drawn as an ER diagram?
x: Conceptual design produces an ER model of entities and relationships that does not depend on the DBMS. Physical design decides how the data will be stored on a chosen DBMS.

q: In which step of database design are decisions made about storage structures, file organisation and indexes on the chosen DBMS?
x: Physical design turns the logical tables into storage details such as indexes and file organisation. Conceptual design does not deal with storage at all.

q: Before any design is drawn, the designers interview the users of a hospital to find out what data they record and what reports they need. This is which step of the database life cycle?
x: Requirements analysis collects the users' data needs; the design steps come after it. Implementation is when the tables are actually created on the DBMS.

q: In an ER diagram, how is the key attribute of an entity usually shown?
o: Its name is written inside the entity's rectangle in capitals
It is drawn as a diamond
It is drawn as a double rectangle
Its name is underlined inside the oval
x: Attributes are drawn as ovals, and the name of the key attribute, such as RollNo, is underlined. Diamonds are used for relationships.

q: The tables are Ward(WardNo, Floor) and Patient(PatientID, Name). Each patient is in one ward, and a ward has many patients. How is this relationship correctly shown in the tables?
o: Add WardNo to Patient as its primary key
Join both tables into one with Floor as the key
Add PatientID to Ward as a foreign key
Add WardNo to Patient as a foreign key
x: In a one-to-many relationship, the key of the "one" side (Ward) goes into the "many" side (Patient) as a foreign key. PatientID cannot go into Ward, because one ward row would need many patient values.

q: The relationship "a teacher teaches a subject to a class" links three entities, Teacher, Subject and Class, at the same time. What is the degree of this relationship?
x: The degree of a relationship is the number of entities taking part: three gives a ternary relationship. Binary relationships link only two entities.

q: In the relationship "an employee supervises other employees", both ends of the relationship are the same entity, Employee. What is this relationship called?
x: A relationship of an entity with itself is unary, also called recursive. A binary relationship links two different entities.

q: An ER diagram shows Customer —places— Order, with 1 on the Customer side and M on the Order side. What does this mean?
o: One customer can place many orders, and each order is placed by one customer
Many customers share every order equally
One order can be placed by many customers together
Each customer can place only one order
x: 1 on Customer and M on Order means a one-to-many relationship from customer to orders, with each order going back to a single customer. The second option reads the cardinality the wrong way round.

q: In an ER model, the number of instances of one entity that can be linked to one instance of another entity is called the relationship's:
x: Cardinality, such as one-to-one or one-to-many, gives how many instances can be linked. The degree of a relationship is the number of entities that take part.

q: The attribute Address of a Student is made of Street, City and Postcode. What kind of attribute is Address?
x: A composite attribute can be divided into smaller attributes. A derived attribute is one that is calculated from another attribute, such as age from date of birth.

q: A Student entity stores DateOfBirth. The attribute Age is not stored but worked out from DateOfBirth whenever it is needed. What kind of attribute is Age?
x: A derived attribute is calculated from other stored data. A composite attribute is divided into parts, which is not the case for Age.

q: An ER design has the entities Student, Course and Teacher. Student and Course are many-to-many; Teacher and Course are one-to-many (a teacher teaches many courses, each course has one teacher). What is the smallest number of tables needed?
x: Each entity needs a table (3), the many-to-many needs one junction table (1), and the one-to-many is shown by a foreign key TeacherID in Course, with no extra table: 3 + 1 = 4. 5 would wrongly add a table for the one-to-many.

q: In the sentence "A customer buys a product", which word becomes a relationship in an ER diagram?
x: Nouns such as customer and product become entities, and the verb that links them, buys, becomes the relationship drawn as a diamond.

q: Student and Course are in a many-to-many relationship through Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID). Each student gets a Grade in each course. Where should Grade be stored?
o: In Student, since each student has a grade
In Course, since each course gives grades
In a separate table keyed on Grade alone
In Enrolment, since it depends on the student and the course together
x: One student has different grades in different courses, so Grade belongs to the pair (StudentID, CourseID) in the junction table. In Student, one row could hold only one grade for all courses.

q: A row is inserted into Student(RollNo, Name, City), where RollNo is the primary key, but RollNo is left empty (NULL). Which rule does this break?
x: Entity integrity says a primary key value must never be NULL, so every row can be identified. Referential integrity concerns foreign keys matching rows in another table.

q: Class(ClassID, Room) has the ClassID values 1, 2 and 3. A row is inserted into Student(RollNo, Name, ClassID) with ClassID = 9, where ClassID refers to Class. Which rule does this break?
x: A foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the related table, and there is no class 9. Entity integrity is about the primary key being NULL, which is not the case here.

q: Class has the rows ClassID 1, 2 and 3. Student has the rows (101, Ali, 1), (102, Sana, 1) and (103, Omar, 3), where the last column is a foreign key to Class. Referential integrity is enforced with no cascading. Which Class row can be deleted?
x: Classes 1 and 3 are referred to by students, so deleting either would leave students pointing to a class that does not exist. No student refers to class 2, so only it can be deleted.

q: The Marks column of a Result table may hold only whole numbers from 0 to 100. A user tries to enter 120. Which kind of constraint stops this?
x: A domain constraint limits a column to its allowed set of values, here 0 to 100. Entity and referential integrity deal with primary and foreign keys.

q: Enrol(StudentID, Name, CourseID, CourseTitle) is keyed on (StudentID, CourseID). Student S5 is the only student in course CS9. When S5's row is deleted, the title of CS9 disappears from the database. This is a:
x: Deleting one fact (S5's enrolment) also removes another fact (CS9's title), which is a deletion anomaly. An insertion anomaly is when a fact cannot be added without unrelated data.

q: Enrol(StudentID, Name, CourseID, CourseTitle) is keyed on (StudentID, CourseID). A new course CS12 cannot be recorded until some student enrols in it. This is a:
x: The course's details cannot be inserted without a StudentID, because part of the key would be NULL. A deletion anomaly loses data when a row is removed, which is not what happens here.

q: A relation R(P, Q, S) has these rows: (1, x, 10), (2, x, 10), (3, y, 20), (4, z, 20). Which functional dependency holds in these rows?
x: Each Q value has one S value: x → 10, y → 20, z → 20, so Q → S holds. S → Q fails because S = 20 appears with both y and z.

q: In a relation, what does the functional dependency P → Q mean?
o: Each value of Q is associated with exactly one value of P
Each value of P is associated with exactly one value of Q
P and Q are both primary keys of the relation
Q is a foreign key that refers to P
x: P → Q says that if two rows have the same P, they must have the same Q. It says nothing about Q determining P, which would be Q → P.

q: Work(EmpID, ProjID, EmpName, Hours) has the key (EmpID, ProjID), with EmpID → EmpName and (EmpID, ProjID) → Hours. Which split puts it into 2NF?
o: Emp(EmpID, EmpName) and Work(EmpID, ProjID, Hours)
x: EmpName depends on only part of the key (EmpID), a partial dependency, so it moves to a table keyed on EmpID; Hours depends on the whole key and stays with (EmpID, ProjID). Putting Hours with EmpID alone loses which project the hours belong to.

q: Student(Roll, Name, DeptID, DeptName) has the key Roll and atomic values, with Roll → Name, Roll → DeptID and DeptID → DeptName. What is the highest normal form it is in?
x: The key is a single column, so there can be no partial dependency and it is in 2NF. DeptName depends on Roll through DeptID, a transitive dependency, so it is not in 3NF.

q: Student(Roll, Name, Phones) has the row (1, Ayesha, "0300-1111111, 0321-2222222"). Which change puts the design into 1NF?
o: Sort the table by Roll in ascending order
Store each phone number in its own row of StudentPhone(Roll, Phone)
Store the numbers without the hyphens
Make the Phones column long enough to hold more numbers
x: 1NF needs one value per cell, so each phone number gets its own row in a separate table linked by Roll. A longer column still holds a list in one cell.

q: Result(Roll, Subject, Marks) has the key (Roll, Subject) and atomic values. Its only functional dependency is (Roll, Subject) → Marks. What is the highest of 1NF, 2NF and 3NF that it is in?
x: Marks depends on the whole key, so there is no partial dependency (2NF), and there is no other non-key attribute for a transitive dependency (3NF). A composite key alone does not break 2NF.

q: A timetable table stores a teacher's phone number in each of the 5 rows for her classes. Her number changes, and it is corrected in only 2 of the rows, so the table now shows two different numbers for her. This is a:
x: When one fact is repeated in many rows, changing it in only some rows leaves the data inconsistent; this is an update anomaly. Nothing was inserted or deleted here.

q: A relation R(P, Q, S, T) has the functional dependencies P → Q, Q → S and P → T. Which single attribute is a key of R?
x: P gives Q and T directly and gives S through Q, so P determines every attribute. Q determines only S, so it cannot identify a whole row.
